title: Motherhood After Breast Cancer: What the Evidence Says About Fertility
excerpt: Treatment, not the cancer itself, is what can threaten fertility — and specialists say preservation before the first chemotherapy cycle, plus trial evidence on pausing hormone therapy, leaves most younger survivors a real path to pregnancy.
body:
• Many women can become mothers after breast cancer treatment. The cancer itself rarely harms fertility — it is chemotherapy and hormone therapy that can damage eggs or delay childbearing.
  • The single most time-sensitive step: raise fertility with your oncologist before treatment starts. Egg or embryo freezing works best before the first chemotherapy cycle.
  • In the POSITIVE trial, about 74% of women who paused hormone therapy after 18–30 months to try for a baby achieved pregnancy, and three-year recurrence was 8.9% for those who paused versus 9.2% in a comparison group.
  • Timing is individual — many clinicians discuss waiting about two years after diagnosis — so the plan has to be made with your own oncology team, not from a general guide.

For a growing number of women, a breast cancer diagnosis now arrives in the same years they had planned to start a family. The question that follows — can I still become a mother? — has a more hopeful evidence-based answer than many expect: in most cases, yes. Specialists stress, however, that the answer depends on decisions made early, often before treatment begins. The Breast Cancer Research Foundation's guide to fertility after breast cancer and Living Beyond Breast Cancer's medically reviewed explainer set out what the research shows.

It Is the Treatment, Not the Cancer, That Affects Fertility

Breast cancer itself does not typically damage the uterus, fallopian tubes or ovaries. The risk comes from treatment. Chemotherapy can damage ovarian follicles — the structures that hold eggs — and one class of drugs, alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide, poses a greater threat than others because it can stop the ovaries producing mature eggs and can cause primary ovarian insufficiency, in which the ovaries stop working before age 40. The absolute numbers are more reassuring than the warning suggests: a meta-analysis of five studies found ovarian insufficiency in 31 of every 100 younger patients after chemotherapy — which means most younger patients avoided it. Age matters throughout: women treated before 35 are more likely to conceive afterwards, because younger women generally have more eggs in reserve.

Hormone therapy works differently. Drugs such as tamoxifen, prescribed for five to ten years for hormone receptor-positive cancer, do not directly damage the ovaries, but they delay childbearing — and fertility falls naturally over those years. Tamoxifen can also harm a fetus, so pregnancy must not happen while taking it; Living Beyond Breast Cancer advises waiting two months after stopping for the drug to clear the body. Radiation therapy aimed at the breast, by contrast, does not raise the risk of infertility, because it is targeted and the scatter reaching the ovaries is too small to cause ovarian failure.

Preservation Works Best Before the First Cycle

Fertility preservation is a conversation for the days right after diagnosis, not after treatment ends. The established options are embryo freezing — eggs retrieved, fertilised and frozen — and egg freezing, in which unfertilised eggs are stored, an approach suited to women without a current partner. Both need roughly two to three weeks of ovary-stimulating medication before retrieval, which is why they may not fit a treatment plan that must start immediately. For estrogen receptor-positive cancers, doctors pair stimulation with letrozole to keep estrogen levels low during the process.

Two further options cover cases the first two cannot. Medication called a GnRH agonist can suppress ovarian activity during chemotherapy to protect the ovaries; in the research summarised by the Breast Cancer Research Foundation, 14 of every 100 patients taking it during chemotherapy experienced ovarian insufficiency. Ovarian tissue freezing — removing and freezing part of the ovary for later reimplantation — is reserved mainly for girls who have not reached puberty and women who must begin treatment within days. Reassuringly, a study co-authored by Dr. Ann Partridge found no difference in five-year invasive disease-free survival between women who did and did not undergo fertility preservation, even allowing for the short delay some procedures require.

What the Pregnancy Evidence Shows

Research following large groups of survivors has consistently found that pregnancy after treatment for early-stage breast cancer does not raise the risk of recurrence or affect survival — including for estrogen receptor-positive disease. A 2023 study published in the journal Cancer found that most participants diagnosed at age 40 or younger, with stage 0 to stage III disease, who tried to conceive were able to get pregnant, and the majority had a live birth.

The strongest evidence on timing comes from the international POSITIVE trial, which followed women with hormone receptor-positive cancer who paused endocrine therapy after 18 to 30 months of treatment to attempt pregnancy, for a break of up to two years. Roughly 74% achieved pregnancy. Three-year recurrence was 8.9% among women who paused, against 9.2% in a matched comparison group — no increase in short-term risk — and five-year follow-up data presented at ESMO confirmed no elevated recurrence hazard from a temporary pause, according to a clinical guide summarising the trial. Participants were expected to resume therapy after the break, and that resumption remains part of the plan.

How Long to Wait, and What to Do Next

There is no single safe interval. Because recurrence risk is highest in the first two years, many clinicians discuss waiting about two years after diagnosis, plus several months after chemotherapy ends so damaged eggs clear and drugs leave the system — but the Breast Cancer Research Foundation notes the safest timing varies by cancer type, recurrence risk and treatment plan, and is individualised. Women who did not preserve fertility before treatment still have routes: many conceive naturally once cycles return, ovarian reserve can be measured with an AMH blood test and a follicle count, and options after treatment include IVF, donor eggs, surrogacy and adoption.

The practical steps are clear. If you are premenopausal and newly diagnosed, raise fertility with your oncologist before treatment begins, even if the doctor does not raise it first, and ask for a referral to a fertility specialist. Cost and access remain real barriers — preservation is expensive, coverage is uneven, and the Breast Cancer Research Foundation notes that Black and Hispanic women face longer waits and greater difficulty obtaining appointments — which is one more reason the conversation cannot wait until treatment is over.
